Asynchronous programming in Python leverages the asyncio event loop to manage concurrent I/O-bound operations without threading overhead. The core abstractions are coroutines, defined with the async def syntax, and awaitables that yield control back to the event loop via the await keyword. When a coroutine encounters an await expression, the event loop suspends its execution and schedules other pending tasks, resuming only when the awaited future resolves. This cooperative multitasking model avoids the race conditions inherent in preemptive thread scheduling. The asyncio.gather function enables structured concurrency by running multiple coroutines simultaneously and collecting their results. Error propagation follows standard exception semantics: if any gathered coroutine raises, the exception surfaces to the caller. For CPU-bound workloads, asyncio integrates with ProcessPoolExecutor via loop.run_in_executor, offloading computation to separate processes while maintaining the non-blocking event loop. Context variables, introduced in Python 3.7 through the contextvars module, provide task-local storage analogous to thread-local data. Libraries such as aiohttp and httpx build on these primitives to deliver fully asynchronous HTTP clients and servers suitable for high-throughput microservice architectures.
